headline: Employees Report Same Figure Appearing in Background of Unrelated Video Calls
subheadline: Blurry shape spotted in at least 847 screenshots across 12 different companies
summary: A growing online community is documenting what they believe is a recurring entity visible only in the backgrounds of video conferences.
content:
It started with a Threadit post titled "Does anyone else see the guy in the background?" What followed has become one of the internet's most unsettling rabbit holes.

Users across multiple platforms have begun sharing screenshots from video calls in which a blurry, humanoid figure appears to be standing in the background of participants' homes or offices. The figure is never in focus, never acknowledged by the call participants, and never appears in the same location twice.

But users insist it's the same figure every time.

"Look at the posture," explained u/BackgroundWatcher in a viral analysis post. "Look at how it's always turned slightly away, like it's pretending not to listen. It's the same thing. It's always the same thing."

The community, which calls itself "Zoom Watchers," has compiled over 847 screenshots from video calls across at least 12 different companies. In each image, the figure appears in what should be an empty space: behind a couch, in a doorway, reflected in a window.

"I pulled up my own Zoom recording from last month," wrote one user. "I live alone. There's something in my hallway in frame 4,847. I never saw it during the call."

Skeptics point out that compression artifacts, lighting conditions, and the human tendency to see patterns in noise could explain the phenomenon. Video call software companies have not commented.

Dr. Patricia Huang, who previously analyzed the Threadit water debate, offered a measured take: "Either thousands of people are experiencing a shared delusion, or there's something in the backgrounds of video calls. Both options are equally concerning."

The original poster has since deleted their account. Their final comment read: "It knows we're looking."
author: Marcus Webb, Internet Culture Correspondent
